stages.title: Advanced grammar
stages.hook: In 'evlerimizden', how many pieces of meaning are packed into one word?
explain: Turkish is agglutinative: suffixes are attached to the stem in a fixed order. 'Ev-ler-imiz-den' = house-PLURAL-our-FROM, 'from our houses'. For nouns the order is plural, possessive, case. For verbs it is roughly negation, tense, person: gel-me-di-m (I did not come).

Vowel harmony chooses the vowel of each suffix. Two-way harmony (e/a): -ler/-lar, -de/-da, -den/-dan. Four-way harmony (i, ı, u, ü): possessives and the past -di/-dı/-du/-dü. Suffix choice depends on the last vowel of the stem: front or back, rounded or unrounded. Consonants harmonise too: -de becomes -te after voiceless consonants.
stages.mnemonic: Ev-ler-imiz-den: one stem, three tiny trains.
sentences: The teachers came to the school.

gq.q: What is the usual order of noun suffixes?

o: The last vowel is back (a), so -a is used
gq.why: Two-way harmony: back vowel takes a.

panel.q: Which form is correct for 'in our books'?
Why is the past of 'git' written 'gitti'?
o: Consonant harmony turns -di into -ti after t

panel.q: What does harmony do in 'gelmedim' vs 'okumadım'?
o: The vowel of -me/-ma and -di/-dı matches the stem
panel.why: Both suffixes harmonise with the stem.

teach.model: Turkish adds suffixes in a fixed order. Nouns take plural, possessive, case. Vowel harmony makes the vowel match the stem; consonant harmony changes d to t.

stages.title: Complex sentence patterns
stages.hook: How can you say 'The book that I read' in Turkish when there is no word for 'that'?
explain: Turkish relative clauses are built with participles placed before the noun. 'The book that I read' is 'okuduğum kitap' (read-I-participle book). The suffix -dığım marks a completed event; for future or unfulfilled events use -eceğim: 'okuyacağım kitap' (the book that I will read). The subject is marked by a possessive ending.

Other patterns: -ip joins actions ('Kalkıp gitti', he got up and left), -erek means 'by doing' ('Çalışarak öğrenir'), -ince means 'when' ('Eve gelince aradı', when he came home he called). 'Diye' introduces quoted thought or purpose: 'Gelecek diye bekledim' (I waited thinking he would come).
stages.mnemonic: Before the noun, not after: the book-that-I-read.
items: the book that I will read
sentences: The book I read was interesting.
When I came home, I called her.

gq.q: Where does a relative clause go in Turkish?
o: At the end of the sentence
gq.why: Turkish places the participle clause before the noun.

panel.q: Why is 'okuduğum kitap' not 'kitap ki okudum'?
o: Turkish uses participle clauses, not a relative pronoun

panel.q: What does 'Eve gelince aradı' mean?
o: When he or she came home, he or she called

panel.q: Which suffix suits an event that has not happened yet?

teach.model: Relative clauses use participles before the noun: okuduğum kitap. Converbs: -ip (and), -erek (by), -ince (when).

stages.title: Extended conversations
stages.hook: How do you disagree politely in Turkish?
explain: In a longer conversation, use fillers and polite openings: 'Bence' (I think), 'Bana göre' (according to me), 'Katılıyorum' (I agree), 'Katılmıyorum' (I disagree). To soften: 'Haklısın ama...' (You are right but...), 'Belki de' (Maybe).

Turn-taking markers: 'Peki' (well, OK), 'Yani' (I mean), 'Tamam' (OK), 'Şey' (um). For clarification: 'Ne demek istiyorsun?' (What do you mean?). The ending -dır adds formality or certainty: 'Öyledir' (That is so). Short echo questions: 'Gerçekten mi?' (Really?), 'Öyle mi?' (Is that so?).
stages.mnemonic: Bence, ama, belki: opinion, contrast, softener.
sentences: I think this is a good idea.
You are right, but I disagree.

panel.q: Why add 'belki' to a statement?
A friend says 'Yani...' and pauses. What is it?
panel.why: Yani is a filler like I mean.

panel.q: Which reply is rude?

teach.model: Use bence for I think and katılıyorum / katılmıyorum for agree and disagree. Soften with haklısın ama and belki.

points.ask: How do I give an opinion?
How do I agree or disagree?

stages.title: Formal and informal registers
stages.hook: Why does Turkish have both 'sen' and 'siz' for one person?
explain: Informal Turkish uses sen with friends, family and children. Formal Turkish uses siz with strangers, elders and officials: 'Nasılsınız?' The same plural form also marks respect. In an email: 'Sayın Bay Yılmaz,' (Dear Mr Yılmaz) ... 'Saygılarımla' (With respect).

Address terms also express respect: abla, abi, hanım, bey. 'Ahmet Bey' and 'Ayşe Hanım' add polite titles after the first name. In speech, Turkish uses 'Buyurun' (Please, go ahead), 'Rica ederim' (You are welcome). The ending -dir can mark formal statements: 'Toplantı yarındır'.
stages.mnemonic: Sen is a handshake you know; siz is a bow you respect.
sentences: Dear Mr Yılmaz, how are you?

gq.q: Which pronoun is formal for one person?
Where do Bey and Hanım go?
o: At the end of the sentence

panel.q: Why is 'Sayın' used in letters?
panel.why: Sayın means Dear in formal letters.

panel.q: Which is correct to a manager you meet first time?
Why do waiters say 'Buyurun'?
o: It invites and offers service politely

teach.model: Sen is informal and siz is formal. Use Sayın, Bey, Hanım and Saygılarımla in formal writing.

points.ask: How do I end a formal letter?

stages.title: Reading articles and literature
stages.hook: How does a Turkish news headline differ from everyday speech?
explain: Headlines often omit verbs or use compact noun phrases and the present tense for past events. Typical connectors: 'ancak' (however), 'ayrıca' (also), 'buna göre' (according to this), 'açıkladı' (announced). The izafet structure links nouns: 'Türkiye Cumhuriyeti' and 'şehir merkezi' (city centre): the second noun takes -i.

Literature: Yunus Emre wrote poetry in the 13th century, Nazım Hikmet became a major modern poet, and Orhan Pamuk won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2006. When you read, find the subject, the final verb, and the case endings that tell you who did what to whom: 'Kediyi köpek kovaladı' (The dog chased the cat).
stages.mnemonic: Find the verb at the end, then ask who did it to whom.
sentences: The author wrote a new novel.

gq.q: What does the accusative -yi in 'Kediyi' show?
Who won the 2006 Nobel Prize in Literature?

panel.q: In 'Kediyi köpek kovaladı', who chased whom?
panel.why: Case endings, not word order, show the roles.

panel.q: Why does izafet add -i in 'şehir merkezi'?
panel.why: Noun-noun compounds mark the second noun.

panel.q: Which connector signals contrast in a news article?

teach.model: Find the final verb first, then use case endings to see who did what. Izafet compounds mark the second noun with -i.

points.ask: Where do I find the verb?

stages.title: Essay and correspondence writing
stages.hook: How do you begin and end a formal email in Turkish?
explain: A formal email follows a pattern: greeting (Sayın Yetkili,), purpose (…ile ilgili yazıyorum), details, request (… rica ediyorum), thanks and closing (Saygılarımla,). Use the formal siz forms: 'Yardımcı olabilir misiniz?' (Could you help?).

For an opinion essay: introduction (giriş), development (gelişme), conclusion (sonuç). Linking: 'Öncelikle' (first of all), 'Ayrıca' (also), 'Sonuç olarak' (in conclusion). Use consistent tense and avoid slang. Check the harmony of every suffix and the apostrophe on proper names: Ankara'da, Ayşe'ye.
stages.mnemonic: Giriş, gelişme, sonuç: three parts, one clear path.
sentences: I am writing about the course.
I would like to ask for help.

gq.q: Which closing is appropriate for a formal email?

panel.q: Why does 'Ankara'da' have an apostrophe?
o: Suffixes on proper names are separated
panel.why: Turkish writes an apostrophe before suffixes on proper names.

panel.q: Which sentence is more polite?
panel.why: The question form with siz is polite.

panel.q: Why should an essay have giriş, gelişme, sonuç?

teach.model: A formal email: Sayın Yetkili, purpose, request, thanks, Saygılarımla. Essays: giriş, gelişme, sonuç with öncelikle, ayrıca and sonuç olarak.

points.ask: How do I open and close?
What are the parts of an essay?

trip.prompt: Look at the structure of a formal letter.

stages.title: Translation fundamentals
stages.hook: Why can't you translate 'He' and 'She' word for word into Turkish?
explain: Turkish has one third-person pronoun 'o' for he, she and it, and no articles or grammatical gender. When translating into English you must choose he or she from context. Going the other way, you add endings and reorder: 'I saw the film yesterday' becomes 'Dün filmi gördüm'.

Translation tips: do not translate word for word; move the verb to the end; check case endings; keep register (sen/siz). False friends: 'sempatik' means likeable, not sympathetic; 'aktüel' means current. Idioms such as 'Eline sağlık' (thanks to the cook) have no word-for-word English equivalent; always translate the meaning.
stages.mnemonic: Translate the meaning, not the words.

gq.q: How many third-person singular pronouns does Turkish have?
gq.why: O covers he, she and it.

o: A word that looks similar but has a different meaning

panel.q: Why must a translator choose he or she?
o: English marks gender, Turkish does not
panel.why: The target language needs more information.

panel.q: Why change word order when translating into English?
o: Turkish is SOV and English is SVO

panel.q: Which is the best strategy for an idiom?

teach.model: Turkish uses o for he, she, it. Reorder SOV to SVO, check case endings, beware false friends, and translate meaning.

stages.title: Regional varieties and cultural context
stages.hook: Is the Turkish in Istanbul the same as the Turkish in the Black Sea region or in Cyprus?
explain: Standard Turkish is based on the Istanbul dialect. Regional varieties include Black Sea speech, Aegean and Eastern Anatolian speech. They differ in intonation, vocabulary and some sounds, but speakers understand each other well. Turkish is also spoken in Northern Cyprus, in parts of the Balkans and by large communities in Germany and elsewhere.

Turkish is a member of the Turkic family, related to Azerbaijani, Turkmen, Kazakh and Uzbek. Azerbaijani is especially close to Turkish. Cultural context matters: hospitality (misafirperverlik), tea culture and kissing the hand of elders at holidays are traditional signs of respect.
sentences: Turkish is spoken in many countries.

gq.q: On which dialect is Standard Turkish based?
gq.why: Istanbul speech is the standard base.

gq.q: Which language is closest to Turkish?

panel.q: Why can speakers of different Turkish dialects understand each other?
o: They share grammar and most vocabulary
panel.why: Differences are mainly accent and some words.

panel.q: Which family does Turkish belong to?
How should a learner treat dialect words?
o: Learn standard Turkish and notice regional forms

teach.model: Standard Turkish is based on Istanbul speech. Regional accents exist but are mutually understandable. Turkish belongs to the Turkic family.

points.ask: What is standard Turkish based on?
Can dialect speakers understand each other?

stages.title: Structured debates and presentations
stages.hook: How do you structure a two-minute presentation in Turkish?
explain: A presentation has an opening (Merhaba, bugün ... hakkında konuşacağım: Today I will talk about ...), main points (İlk olarak, ikinci olarak: First, second) and a close (Dinlediğiniz için teşekkür ederim: Thank you for listening). Eye contact and clear pauses help.

In a debate, use stance phrases: 'Bu görüşe katılmıyorum çünkü...' (I do not agree with this view because...). Rebuttal: 'Ancak şunu unutmamalıyız' (However, we should not forget...). Use 'siz' with the audience. Avoid fillers like 'yani' too often. Always end with a clear summary.
sentences: Today I will talk about water.

panel.q: Why use siz with an audience?
o: It is a rule of grammar

panel.q: Which structure is clearer?
panel.why: A clear structure helps the audience.

panel.q: Why avoid overusing 'yani'?
panel.why: Too many fillers weaken a talk.

teach.model: Open with a topic statement, give your points with ilk olarak and ikinci olarak, and close with a thank you. In debate use katılmıyorum çünkü... and ancak....
